questions.stem: The reagent that detects hydrolysis progress is

options.explanation: Ag+ precipitates liberated halide ions, timing the C-X bond breaking.
That reagent drives substitution, not this rate test.
Unrelated to halide detection here.
No acid-base endpoint is timed.

questions.stem: The water bath temperature for the hydrolysis race is

options.explanation: Far below the specified bath.
The set bath keeps all three tubes at the same temperature.
The method specifies the warm bath.
Too hot for the set-up as specified.

questions.stem: Ethanol is mixed into the test tubes because

options.text: It speeds the silver nitrate's reaction
options.explanation: The silver chemistry is unaffected; ethanol only aids dissolving.
Precipitate colours come from the silver halides.

options.text: It dissolves the halogenoalkanes into the reacting mixture
options.explanation: The co-solvent brings the organic substrate into contact with the aqueous silver nitrate.

options.text: It reacts with the halide ions
options.explanation: Ethanol takes no reacting part.

questions.stem: A precipitate forms in these tubes because

options.explanation: No such solidification occurs.

options.text: Silver nitrate reacts with the whole halogenoalkane directly
options.explanation: Silver reacts with liberated halide, not the intact C-X bond.

options.text: The water bath freezes the mixture
options.explanation: The bath warms, not freezes.

options.text: Hydrolysis liberates halide ions that silver ions catch as insoluble silver halide
options.explanation: Ag+ + X- -> AgX(s) is the visible clock.

questions.stem: Starting three stopwatches simultaneously matters because

options.text: The precipitate times must share a common start to rank the rates fairly
options.explanation: A common zero makes the three clocks comparable.
No such decomposition drives the timing.

options.text: The bath temperature changes every minute
options.explanation: The bath holds temperature steady.
They form gradually - that is the whole measurement.

questions.stem: State the mixture held in each test tube.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol mixed with acidified aqueous silver nitrate, plus a few drops of the halogenoalkane.

questions.stem: State what is timed in each tube.
questions.modelAnswer: The time taken for the silver halide precipitate to appear.

questions.stem: Explain why faster precipitate formation indicates faster hydrolysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Halide ions appear only as fast as the C-X bond breaks; silver catches them immediately, so the precipitate clock mirrors the hydrolysis rate.

questions.stem: One tube's precipitate appears in 20 s, another's in 200 s. Which halogenoalkane is in the faster tube, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The 20 s tube holds the iodoalkane: its weak C-I bond breaks fastest, liberating iodide and precipitating silver iodide soonest.

questions.stem: Which silver halide precipitate appears fastest in the hydrolysis race?

options.explanation: AgF is soluble - no precipitate forms at all.
The weakest C-I bond liberates iodide fastest.
The strongest C-Cl bond breaks slowest.
Bromide middles the ladder.

questions.stem: No precipitate forms for fluoroalkanes because

options.explanation: C-F is the strongest bond and reacts slowest or not at all.
AgF exists; it is just soluble.

options.text: Silver fluoride is soluble in the reaction medium
options.explanation: No insoluble AgF can accumulate visibly.
They form; they simply stay dissolved with Ag+.

questions.stem: The order of halogenoalkane reactivity by halogen is

options.explanation: That reverses the bond-enthalpy logic.
C-F is strongest, so fluoroalkanes are least reactive.

options.text: All equal, as each carries one halogen
options.explanation: The halogen identity changes the bond strength decisively.

options.text: Iodoalkane > bromoalkane > chloroalkane, with fluoroalkane least
options.explanation: Bond enthalpy falls down the group, so reactivity rises.

questions.stem: Comparing 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane hydrolysis rates, the fastest is

options.explanation: Tertiary hydrolyses quickest of the three classes.
Primary hydrolyses slowest here.
Secondary middles the class trend.
Class changes the rate even at fixed halogen.

questions.stem: Which variables must stay constant in the primary-secondary-tertiary comparison?

options.explanation: Fair comparison requires the controls.

options.text: The halogen stays the same and the overall formula does too
options.explanation: Both are named as the controls for the class comparison.

options.text: The halogen and the carbon class
options.explanation: The carbon class is the variable, not a control.

options.text: The water bath and the solvent only
options.explanation: Those matter too, but the named controls are halogen and formula.

questions.stem: State the colours and speed order of the three silver halide precipitates.
questions.modelAnswer: White AgCl slowest, cream AgBr middle, pale yellow AgI fastest.

questions.stem: State the prediction for silver astatide.
questions.modelAnswer: Silver astatide would form even more quickly than silver iodide, one step further down the group.

questions.stem: Explain why the C-I bond breaks fastest in hydrolysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Of the carbon-halogen series the C-I bond surrenders at the lowest enthalpy, so least energy is needed to break it and iodide ions form first.

questions.stem: A same-halogen race uses 1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Predict the order and name the controlled variable that makes the race fair.
questions.modelAnswer: The tertiary 2-bromo-2-methylpropane precipitates first, primary 1-bromobutane last; fairness requires the same halogen (bromine) and the same molecular formula C4H9Br in both tubes.
